blocks.x: This is September the 29th, 1956, and I'm at 815 Alleen Street, New Orleans, Louisiana, and I'm having an informal chat with Arnold Ayacana. Arnold, give me your full name. Is Arnold the whole business? No, it's Arnold Joseph Ayacana. And, of course, if you were a lady,

I wouldn't dare ask you this, but what's the date of your birth? Well, it's August 13th, 1889. Were you born in New Orleans? Born in New Orleans. What street, do you know? I was born on Magazine Street. Magazine in what? Near Thalia. And how many brothers and sisters did you have? Well, I had four brothers and three sisters. And how many are living today? Well, I have three brothers living, three brothers and sisters. And how many of that group were musical? Well, almost all of them played. Pretty many of them played in the house. They don't play anymore hardly except Joe. I don't know what Jack is doing. He's in Chicago. But Joe is playing bass with Amarico. I know that. He still looks fine.
He's very, very incidentally. I ran into him down at a radio shop the other day. He was buying some
material for an aerial he was putting up. Yeah, he could drink and should have done that years ago. I was drinking. Oh, he's been off it now about six years.
Ah. We're drinking more. Arnold, what instruments did you all play in the family?
Well, guitar and fiddle, piano, bass. That's mostly no except for Joe and Jack. They played trombone.
Both of them played trombone? At the same time. No reed, huh? No reed. Did you all take lessons or just a family thing?
Well, it was more or less a family thing. I took lessons on the piano and then when I went to Chicago, I took lessons on the bass again.
Well, how old were you when you started playing music?
I was six.
What instrument?
Bass.
And how could you stand up to a bass?

Well, you remember the old sewing machine covers they used to have? Those little boxes. I used to get on top of that box. And I had a small bass. I guess it was about, oh, not a half size, about a quarter size.
You started out on that?
Yes, I did.
And were you strong enough to press the strings down?
Oh, sure, sure. I developed into a real cat.
Did you all have a kids band?
Well, we had a kids band with Jack Lane.
I mean, youngsters?
Yes, all the old short pants.
I'll be doggone.

Oh, yeah. George Brunus was in that band and Pansy Lane, Jack's son, and myself. I don't know just who else. But you see... About how old were you then? Oh, I was about 14. Jack lived on Port Street. And we used to go down there and stay overnight. We'd play a job Saturday night and stay at his house. And then we'd catch the Smokey Mary on a Sunday morning and go out and play at Millenburg. When you were kids at it?
Yeah, sure. Did you get paid?
Sure we got paid. How much? Oh, a dollar, a dollar and a half. That's all anybody got.
Did they give you something to eat and something to drink, beer and stuff like that?

Well, no, they wouldn't give us any beer, because at that time they wouldn't give any kids anything that was alcoholic. They'd give you all that popping stuff, you know, cream soda and the big old fresh and butter.
Oh, you could eat there on that Millenburg, huh?
Oh, sure. Well, incidentally, that's where Jack Lane got the name Papa Lane and Mama Lane.
Putting the kids up.
Yeah, yeah. Or George Brunus used to go sleep up in the loft.
Sure. Wasn't he playing an alto then?

No, you see, they all started, those fellas all started, there wasn't any of those boys in that family that played any string instruments. They played all brass. And they used to, well, they had a band, do you remember the Detroit's, Johnny Detroit and Paul? Well, they used to parade in Dust Street out there with a wash tub for a big strum. And I think that, uh, didn't they live up around the, uh,
Arabella Street barn? You mean the Detroit's?

No, the, uh, Brunus's. Brunus's? No. At that time the old man had a place on Chappatula Street, a saloon. And the Brunus's, uh, Chappatula's in what? Well, that was between Josephine and Jackson. And I'm pretty sure that the Brunus's lived on Josephine Street. And they're in the same neighborhood, huh? Oh, yeah. On the Irish Channel? Yeah, yeah. We used to go up there and
rehearsal in the old man's saloon. Well, my memory of those kids of the Brunus's, the two, the two that I knew just by sight, was that one of them played an alto and the other one played a trumpet.

Well, Georgie played alto and he played baritone. He did? Yes, he was a little kid. He used to march in the bands, playing baritone. Incidentally, I used to play drum. You did, huh? Yeah, that's something you didn't know. Oh, I sure did.
Well, wasn't there one of those Brunus's that was so small they called him Stick Pin?

Oh, I... Or was that somebody else? No, I don't remember, I don't remember calling him that. Of course, he called a lot of worse names, but I don't remember calling him that. Now, let's come back to your family. Did your
mother and father play instruments? My father did.

What did he play? He played guitar. He did. Now, was he good? Well, I guess you'd call him good for those days. But your memory of his playing was he was all right? Oh, yes. He played the right key and everything. I mean, he didn't interpose any chords and stuff like they do today. It's all advanced. Straight stuff. Yes, he played only straight. They used to be fellas, I don't know whether you ever heard of the Werleins. Sure. Did you? George Werlein? Yeah. Jack Werlein? Yeah. Julie Oates? No, I don't remember. Oh, you never heard of him? Well, they had a three-piece band too. Bud used to play with them. Up in the Irish Channel? No, they lived on Gainey Street, Gainey near Constance, between Constance and Magazine. Oh, and I was just a kid then. Whenever I played any job, somebody usually had to carry the bass. Well, when you started playing the bass
as a kid, how'd you do about lugging that thing around? Well, I didn't carry it.

What happened? Usually, one fella'd carried a box, a soap box. Remember those wooden boxes, milk boxes, magnolia milk and all that? Well, he'd carry that, then usually Bud would carry the bass. Because Bud, for being a guitar player, I'd carry his guitar. Was he huskier than you were? Oh, yeah. Bud was a big man. He weighed all of 185 pounds for 5'10".
Uh-huh. He was husky. Well, before you actually got good enough to play with those kids' bands, did you all just play in the neighborhood? Did you have a little band that would make up in the

neighborhood? Well, I tell you, we had an old-fashioned player piano. And we used to get my nephew to pump it. Well, she had a pump it pedal, do you remember that? Yeah. And Joe and Jack would get out their horns and I'd get the bass fiddle and we'd play along with the old-fashioned piano. My nephew would paddlet.
Mm-hmm. And then, uh, then you started going out on regular jobs, huh? How long did you all practice
together before you went out? Well, Joe didn't play in a band with me.
Well, uh, that little group that you mentioned that went out to, uh, Millenberg and, uh, dances and all that.
Well, as far as I can remember, we never did have any rehearsals to play that stuff. We knew all that
stuff. I mean, you had to wake yourself into it. You can't just suddenly get on the bass and play.

Oh, well, Jack Lane was the cause of that. He called up all the kids and told them to meet at his house. We'd meet at his house and he had a pretty good-sized front room. So we'd play a couple of tunes and every man for himself. Mm-hmm. Of course, uh, you take in those days, the, the fellas that played music had sharp ears. You couldn't, uh, you couldn't variate a fraction of a tone unless somebody detected it. And the ears were so good that, uh, well, I'd say they played perfect pitch. And they really didn't need much rehearsal because of the fact that the band's ahead of us. Uh, I remember the time when I got, I got beat, banked. I was passing by and, uh, I heard of Dixieland Band was Ragdime Band that time. I sat on the curtain, forgot what time it was. I was sitting there listening to it. Where was that? I came from Wall Magazine Street.
Uh, I was gonna ask you that thing. Do you remember the names of any of the tunes that you

played when you were with those youngsters? Oh, well, they, they, uh, those, those days, there wasn't any names to those tunes. They were numbers and, I mean, like number two, that was a tiger rag, you know. And these fellas attached names to them later on. But, uh, they, there's some, some, uh, titles of the tunes were vulgar, too, as you know. Take your hand off a kid's ass. Yeah. And what else? Well, who stole the lock off the shithouse door, you know,
such stuff as that. So, uh. There was, did Palomar have another name? No, I don't. Somebody mentioned that, I think the name was The Walking Dance.

I don't remember that. I don't remember that. What's this, uh, tune that Jack Glenn refers to his prolly? Do you remember that? Oh, yes. Let's see how that went. I forgot now. I forgot just how it. It hasn't been taken and made up into another tune now. No, not that I know of.
Uh-huh.

And, uh, King Watsky, I told you about him the other day, he, uh, he composed a tune called Ratification. And that was the high, the high-ranking tune around here. It was. Yeah, those that could play it. And a lot of them couldn't play it.
Did it have two or three, uh, key changes in it? Just two, F and B flat. Uh,

uh, we copied more or less because we were interested in the music. It's just like a kid being interested in baseball. Uh, most of us would rather play the music than play baseball. Uh-huh. Y'all loved it, every one of y'all? Oh, sure. Sure. It's the dream music.
Well, uh, how long did you play bass before you took up piano?

Well, I had played piano before I played bass. I was started about the same time, uh, a woman in the neighborhood was teaching me piano at that time. Well, you remember her name? No, right offhand, I don't. She lived nearby you? She lived two doors from me. Pay lessons your folks sent you? Yes, I think it was 50 cents a lesson. But she used to spend about

an hour there. My family put me on a guitar when I was my grandmother, when I was eight years old. And, uh, for about four lessons, this woman came up the house and gave me a lesson. And then she told my mother and daddy I was hopeless, never mind fooling with it. So then I put it down for two years. And then I started going to dances where they had nigger bands, you see. And then I wouldn't dance, I'd just stand up and watch them. Yeah. Yeah. But you're saying how much it cost you. And I got a little bit older. I used to go over across the Bay St. Louis to pass Christian in the summer. And the nigger in the back there that played both guitar and man, and they used to let me pay him two bits an hour just to sit down and let him play along, me and him play together at his house. Yeah. You never did play with any coons, did you know? No. Was it a sharp color line? No,

it wasn't exactly that. It wasn't necessary. And another thing is, there were few colored around where I lived. It was more of a select neighborhood. And on top of that, we had to beat the bell at night. Mm-hmm. You had to beat it to what town? Oh, yeah, nine o'clock. Uh-huh. Every night the fire bell would ring at nine o'clock and we'd have to...
The curfew? The center? Yes, sir. And what about your family? They laid down the law,
that had to be? Oh, yes. It had to be, uh, it had to be down there, at least down at the house. And when they went inside, they locked up, you were locked out. Is that so? Not like today.
Oh. Well, uh, I'll bet you those kids got in very little trouble compared to what they're doing.

Oh, well, there was practically no trouble. Once in a while, one out of a hundred might decide to crack a Chinaman's windowpane or something, you know, something like that. But, uh, as a rule, I'd say 99 percent of the kids were kids. They didn't, uh, well, they were taught better. There wasn't any reason to go around and throw rocks at the feet. Where'd you go to school, uh, um? I went to Jackson School. Did you? Toxico Magazine. Uh-huh. How far'd you go in school? I went to Top. And I went, uh, when I went there, we had an orchestra, school orchestra. And fellas like Gussie Miller, Eddie Edwards, they were in it. Ellie Coulon, he was in it. I have to laugh when those guys tell me how young they are, you know?
What year was that? Do you remember?
Oh, Lord, let's see. That would be about, uh...
Before 1900?

No. That'd be about, uh, 1905, I guess. Something like that. Of course, you see, the first day I had, my, I was taught at home by my sisters. Oh, they did? Give me a fortune. First day I went to school, I went to third grade. Ah. And the third grade was a lot more severe in those days than it is today. Ah. In other words, my comparison with the teaching today would be about, uh, third grade would be equivalent to fifth. Mm-hmm. And they had that split season deal.
They didn't teach music in the schools, though, did they?

Well, oh, yes. Not like today, no. They didn't give much time, about 15 minutes, but, uh, all of that training, that music training, was, uh, by a music teacher with a blackboard and notes. Mm-hmm. On the backboard.
How did you learn your solfeggio? Is that what you learned?
Oh, yes. Yes.
At school?
Yes.
Well, hadn't you learned it before that, though, at all?
Well, sure. I, they sent me to the Milano Conservatory in the old French opera.
They did? Oh, yeah.

Oh, and how? What age? Well, I was just a kid, I guess about seven years old. They had an old gang of kids learning to play at that time, and there was a little fellow lived up on Richard Street. I can't think of what his name is right now, but he and I, we led the field. We, we were in a class by ourselves. So we used to go on Saturday morning early because of the fact that there's only two of us capable of, uh, staying in that class. The rest of them, uh, didn't advance as fast as we did.
Well, at that, uh, class you went to, uh, was it still, uh, learning how to read and all that, or did you actually play music?
Oh, no, we didn't play. No, at that time I was learning violin. Fiddle. Sure.
What else can you play?
Well, uh, I can't play much of anything anymore, but I did play fiddle and mandolin, guitar, bass, piano, drum.
You never fooled with any wind?
No, bass, no. No, I tried to.
You were on the tuba?

Oh, I played tuba, oh yeah. Well, you see, when I played tuba, I went about it right. It had to be that way because, uh, I, uh, I studied with Hamburg, tuba player, and Hamburg was second base in the Chicago Symphony, under stock. So, uh.
Well, how old were you when you took up the tuba?
Oh, I guess that would be about 27, 28.
So you were that old.
Yeah.
You were already on the road, though.

Oh, yes. Well, you see, that was in Chicago. Uh-huh. That was the time when, uh, when the bands were using tuba. So I figured they weren't using much bass fiddles anymore, and that it let, well, it reduced the feel down to only a few chances of playing. So before they did, before they came to the climax, I was ready. I went to Hamburg and I bought myself a tuba, and I started taking lessons from him, and naturally I knew all the music and everything. The only thing I had to worry about was the keys and the lip, pressure on the lip to make the different tones, you know. The rest of it I could read. Well, in a short while I was playing with Buddy Fisher, playing both tuba and string bass, and for which I was compensated with additional money, doubling money. Uh-huh. But I was still in Chicago? Oh, yeah.
Well, let's come back to the Orange Wheel ahead of us ourselves, don't we? Uh, supposedly said that you were around 17 or 18 years old. You were playing a lot of music then, huh?
Oh, yes, yes. Yes.
Did you have a regular outfit then?

No, you see, Jack Lane, he practically had the city sewed up as far as musicians are concerned and workers are concerned. So there wasn't an overabundance of good men. Of course they used to call them squeegees. The guys that really couldn't hit the ball, they called squeegees. Uh, they did call, referred to fiddle player as a squeegee fiddler. Well, he had no bow technique or anything, and he'd get off on tones and things like that. Well, I wanted to ask you too, when you were a kid
playing bass, did you use a bow? Oh, yes. When did you start slapping it? Do you remember?
Well, that's, uh, when I joined the Rhythm Kings, about 1922. Uh-huh. Well, when you, when you were with

Jack Lane's, you were with Jack Lane's outfit here in the audience, playing there, and he had all that bunch of bands. You would march too? You marched with the bands? Oh, yes. But you see, they never did put all

the kids together in the street band that I can remember. Discount them through? Yes. Carnival time, Jack Lane had rolled practically all of the bands that he could gather together to make it, see. And, uh, that's all they played was Dixieland, because that's all they knew. Uh-huh. Nothing else. Well,
then, for dance, it's the same thing. They split them up, the kids? Oh, no. Sometimes all the kids played

with, uh, possibly two grown-ups, the old man Lane, Jack. Uh, I remember when, when I had a fight with Pansy on the Canal Street Fern. You see, he cut this, see that cut? Yeah, you told me about that. How'd that happen? Well, he, he was looking for trouble, and I tried to give it to him. Before I could put it on his jaw, he ripped me with a knife. I didn't know he had a knife. Well, you're damn lucky you didn't cut your tendons, man. Well, I was lucky, because I had this hand straight up. Of course, in those days, I could fight, too, and he knew it. So, I guess that's why he came after me with the knife. He wouldn't have stood a chance as far as, uh, battling was concerned, because I worked out with all of these fighters around here. I used to work out with Kid Greaves and Joe Mandots. All, all the good fighters down there along in J.C. What was your weight then? 126? No, I read, yeah, that's around the featherweight limit, but I, I had, uh, one fight, and then my mother told Louis Bernier that, uh, you fought professionally one time? Yeah, I used to go down and take a beating every day after school, but I learned to fight. I learned to protect myself. Uh, I used to, uh, train with the champion Phantom of the South, Jack Hurley. He later became a great fighter. Well, he was then, too, when I worked with him. He taught me lots, and, well, I didn't, I tell you, if my folks would let me go, I might have been, uh, been the featherweight champion of the world. Yeah. Because I got so working out with these different fellas that it was a question of defend yourself or take it, and I didn't want to get hit any more oftener than, uh, than was necessary. Yeah, you know how many of them were walking on their heels, all those good things. Oh, yeah, but they couldn't hit me solid. None of them hit me solid. None of them ever knocked me down, and, and I worked out with those fellas for about two years. I loved it, liked to fight. So, after a while, my mother, I had me all sewed up with Louis Buenier while they bored me out of the place. I decided that I did gain something out of the whole experiment anyway, because of the fact that I could fight. I could defend myself. I never went around looking for any trouble with anybody, uh, but when, uh, anybody looked for trouble with me, they got it. You know, uh, uh, Pansy played a con, man? Uh, Pansy Lane, he played drums at that time. He did? Oh, yeah, it was years and years later before he ever took a, he used to play, uh, he used to play, uh, peck horn, yeah, he played in the band. Half the time he wouldn't play, he was too lazy. Just walk along, because his daddy was the boss. Now, tell me about, a little bit about your memory of
Jack style. I never let him play, uh, uh, drum. Do you remember it at all? Oh, Jack Lane? Yeah. Well, you mean orchestra, huh? No, I mean band work, either for dance or for, uh, marching.

Marching? Marching, yeah. Well, uh, he, he's, uh, he played, uh, steady, uh, nothing, uh, sensational. Didn't drag? No, nothing sensational. No. He, he played a good rhythmic, uh, bass drum and a, uh,
real steady beat. I have pictures of him in two different parades. One of them, he's playing the

bass drum. Yeah. The other one, he's playing the snare. Yeah, well, it was his choice, yes, either one. Oh, you see, Jack, Jack was never considered a good Dixieland drummer. When you, when you start figuring out, uh, fellas like Pete Mazzarina, and Rag Baby Stevens, and Diddy Stevens, and, uh, Paul Detroit, Johnny Stein, guys of that type that really, well, I remember the time when Diddy Stevens, you see, they had ten men for a carnival parade band, and, uh, Diddy Stevens would make those niggers dance just by playing the march. Didn't need the band. He did. Oh, did you know at that time that the, there was a fellow with a billiard cue used to beat those niggers back? No. Oh, sure, that was, uh, oh, they'd kill each other. Second lining for y'all. Yeah, they wanted to get in. Well, he was a hot band. They, you see, uh, Sellatex, the Sellatex Corporation, and, uh, I, I don't know whether it was a police band. I don't quite remember. Uh, this Italian fella that had an Italian brisilleri outfit. They were dressed like the brisilleris. Well, that's where the Majotas learned to play, too. But they played strictly march music. And none of the niggers wanted to get around, get around these guys, because there was nothing to it. Just a march. And, uh, they used to call Jack Lane's first band was a Reliance band. Because the niggers would call it the Rillians. Let me get at the Rillians band. They'd all rush in there. Had to take clubs and beat them back, separate them. Sure. Uh, what about the
first group that played in the Reliance band? That's Aviga on trumpet, was he? Well, you see,

I don't ever remember of Jack only having one band. Uh, he had, well, like I said before, he had the cream of the crop and he could switch them around. And he was fair about the whole thing. He had several trumpet players and well enough to make four or five bands. And instead of giving one man all the work, he'd switch. He had a fellow named Pete D. Tran. Played terrific trumpet, too. Uh, wasn't there a valve trombonist that played with... Oh, Bill Gallaty. Yeah, he was the champ. I never heard anybody play like him. Was he the daddy of this Gallaty boy that played? Bill Gallaty playing trumpet, yeah. Yeah. They. You see this, Pete D. Tran's, I never seen a man yet play a trumpet on the side of his mouth. That's the way he played it. That's the way he learned to play it. That's the way he got his ambassure. And he couldn't play in the center. But Vega, oh, Louis Armstrong at his best, uh, Buddy Bull, or any of them. None of them topped Vega in my category. That's, uh... No, sir. Not only I, but many, many other old-time musicians will swear that Vega was the greatest. He had it all over these other fellas, uh, because of the fact that he read music, the first start off. And you talk about hitting Cs, Ds, and E's above the staff. He did that when I was a kid. Oh, yes. He used to play tunes like the Wild Cherry Rag and the Black and White Rag. It was real difficult to play. I mean, it was, it was difficult even for a string. And yet he used to run those things to death. Uh, what about this
fantastic story about this fella by the name of Willie Guitar who played the bass and lived on music?
That's true. Is that true? Yeah, that's true. He played in Jack's band too? Yeah, sometime he wore a red
flannel under shirt too. That's true. In the summertime. Well now, uh, what's, uh, the outfit that you remember, uh, that you played with in your audience before you left here?

Yeah, before you left there? Oh, well, I was working with Tommy Brown then. Uh, Tommy Brown in a regular outfit. Yeah, I was playing guitar with him. Uh, huh. You see? They had, uh, Gus Miller on clarinet, Raymond Lopez on trumpet, Tommy Brown on trombone, Bill Lambert on drums, and Steve Brown on bass, and myself on guitar. That was a band. Well, those days, Tommy had cut deeply into Jack Lane, uh, as far as work is concerned. We had quite a bit of work, and we got more money that, uh, Tommy Brown than we did with Jack. Mm-hmm. For the same number of hours. Mm-hmm. But as you know,
a dollar and a half all day long at Millenburg or West End. What about baseball games? You all played out the Ironman Park?
Well, I can't quite remember vividly whether we did or not. I suppose we did, because we played everything around here and across the river, Metry and all in there. We played at, uh, what's the name

of that park in Metry? Uh, it begins with an E, I think. It's no longer there. Oh, is that Lecter Park? No, it's another one. Right over there, uh, Eastman? Eastman. Yeah. You played there? Oh, yes. We played all that. Sometime or rather we played all around. Did you all ever play any of the pretendy dances at Tulane?

That I don't remember of ever playing up there. What about prize fights? Well, yes. We played on the wagon for prize fights. You never played in the fight? In the inside? No, there wasn't any reason to have a band in there at that time. Oh, yeah. I've heard Shillings, any number of times. Well, that must have been later on. I mean, because, uh... Oh, it was later on. I would say it was maybe around 1920, around that... Oh, yeah. That was later. I remember that, uh, later on they played in, but I don't ever remember playing inside, even when Lou Rose had the Winter Garden. I used to put the fights on there. Yeah. That's on Barone Street. Yeah. That's right. We never did play in there, and that was a good place. They had a big stage where the, uh, ring was set up, and it had a box
they could have given us to play. You never did play down to Dauphine Theater, either, did you?
Dauphine Theater. I don't know whether we did or not. I'm not sure on that score.
That's where Sophie Tucker made her debut in New Orleans, you know, down there. Oh, yeah. Well,
the Dauphine used to be a pretty good theater. I don't remember playing there. We might have. We

played everything else. I guess we played the Dauphine, too. Mm-hmm. Well, then, uh, when, uh, 1915 came along, the district was still open down there. Incidentally, did you play in the district at all?
I worked down there. I think I was something for somebody that was sick. I never cared for that
kind of work, Doc. Well, was there one of these places like the Pup or the Cadillac or the Sousie?

Well, uh, that was for Peggy Anstead. Uh-huh. I think that was Iberville and Franklin. Yeah. And, uh, the, the Brunus was playing that. Merritt. Yeah. And Henny. And I was playing piano with them. Mm-hmm. At that time. No, that's been a long time ago. Did you ever play at the halfway house? Uh, for steady, you mean? No. No, I mean even the sub subbing for somebody. Oh, yeah. I played several times out there, but not as a steady job. You see, I didn't care for those long hours. What about Bucktown?

Bucktown, plenty of times. Plenty of times. I wonder if, uh, I'm correct in my memory. The one place they had those dances was up on stilts and they had one door and one pair of steps leading down and there was

fights that started around there all the time. Well, there used to be Bruning's Pavilion. Yeah. The Brunings were the sheriffs out there. Anybody started a fight got beat up and put in jail. They broke the fighting up pretty quickly. That's Bruning, not Brunus. Bruning. No, not Brunus. Bruning. Nah. They had a little tiny old footbridge across the 17th Street Canal at that time.

What about this place near City Park over the Rhine? You ever remember that place there? No. It was a restaurant right across from there. They had a bar and a restaurant there. I didn't play there, no. Did you ever play out at, uh, what do you call that?
Rock Over the Rhine, do you ever remember that place there?
No.
There was a restaurant right across from there, and they had a bar and a restaurant there.
I didn't play there, no.
Did you ever play out at, what do you call that, nickel dance place at West End? I mean, yeah, at West End, they had that, the Tranchina's restaurant.
Oh, yes, yes.
And across from this, right across the street from it was this nickel dance place. You ever played?
Yes, I played out there.
You ever got a Vizedoffer's outfit, wasn't it?

Vizedoffer? Yeah. Well, Brown played out there too, but it looked like the band, when they had Raymond and Gus Miller and Lambert and those, they didn't care for those hard jobs. They were all trying to suck along on the easy work.
Uh-huh. Well, was there any rule, like play a half hour and quit ten, and you'd play a lot until

you'd rest a lot of hours? Oh, no, it wasn't a question of play tired until you'd rest even. Uh, when they had lawn parties and balls and, well, as a matter of fact, any kind of music that you might play in any of those places, you played according to how the crowd was. Many lawn parties would come up and stop the band because the more you played, the less they drank. Uh-huh. And the less they drank, the less money the club made. So naturally, when you played for those clubs, they would tell you to stop and, whoa, there's nothing. 10 or 15 minutes, play 15, rest 15 at that time. But, uh, there wasn't any, uh, limitations set on how much to play and how much to take off. And, uh, there was a lot of fun. Not at that time, there wasn't. I know many times when we played out in the channel there, we played those lawn parties, the pitch battles start about 11.30 and that was the end. That was the end of the party. Oh, yeah, the band usually, sure, the band usually played up on a shed, you know, about seven, eight feet from the ground. And when he started throwing pop bottles and beer bottles and whiskey bottles, it's time to get on the back way.
Down the back. Uh, then, uh, what happened when you all left for Chicago? How'd the whole business start as far as you remember?

Well, I'm positive on that because, uh, you see, we were playing on a tailgate, on a wagon. And, uh, a fella named, uh, a fella named Joe Gorham, uh, a woman dancer by the name of Myrtle Howard. And she was appearing at West End. At that time, they had a theater out there. Yeah. And she was a big-time act. So this fella asked us if we'd consider going to Chicago. Well, he just heard you the one time on the wagon? That's all. He only heard about two tunes and that was it. Uh-huh. He, we were sold. So, he made an appointment. And, uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor.
Uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor.

Uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor. He, we were sold. So, he made an appointment. And instead of Tommy Brown going to see Myrtle Howard, who was staying at the Old Groomall Hotel, Raymond Lopez and I went to see her. Raymond did the talking. And we were, uh, ordered the job right away. In the meantime, Joe Gorham had got in touch with Smiley Carbett and told him where to find the air. And so, Carbett says, All right. And said, send the transportation. Well, he sent the transportation. And that time, it took us 29 hours to ride it. Uh-huh. I think it was 1850 round trip.
Was that called the Panama Limited then, still? No.

No, I don't remember it being called the Panama Limited at that time. They, uh, they had one good train. But, uh, I think that was an extra fare train. I think, I'm pretty sure the fare was 1850 round trip.
Well, who, uh, then when you all spoke to, uh, the lady, what's her name? Oh, Myrtle Howard?
Yeah. And she, uh, you all made arrangements with her at the...
Oh, yeah. Yeah. You gonna back her up or what? No, no. No, no.
No, no. No, no. We were to go up there as a band. I know.
This was an attraction. Not with her act.

No, no. No, no. No, she had two good bookings to fool around with us. She, she didn't want anything like that. Uh, she was a, she was a big, big, big, big Vortigil star. Mm-hmm. She was appearing here. But, uh, she was instrumental through her manager, Gorham, getting us up to Chicago. Mm-hmm. And when we went to Chicago, we... Wait a minute, now, who, who was the whole band? Well, it was, uh, Lopez on trumpet, Gus Miller on clarinet, Tommy Brown on trombone, I was playing piano, and Bill Lambert on drums. There's no bass. Mm-hmm. So we went at five.
Uh-huh. Well, now, uh, was, it went under the name of Brown's Band?
It was Brown's Band, yes.
But they didn't call it Brown's Band from Dixieland then at that time?
No, no, no. They, uh, they, we left here with Raymond Lopez. Uh-huh. Not Tommy Brown. Raymond was the boss. Raymond was the boss.
Raymond was the boss.
That's right. Uh-huh. Raymond was the boss.
Uh-huh. And then, uh, you all went to Chicago and opened up where?
Opened up at the Lamb's Cafe. Ran off on Clark.
How long the contract you had?

Well, as far as they were concerned, they went to Chicago. They were concerned. They wanted to give us a contract the rest of our life at that particular time. Uh, after about four or five weeks. But the start of, the start of the thing was, we followed a gypsy string ensemble in there. So you can imagine what those guys blowing their brains out.
What kind of a looking place was it?
Oh, beautiful place.
I mean, what, marble floors and?
Well, it was tile floor and marble all around the sides. And, uh, every note you'd hit would reverberate back about six times.
Was that a bar in there or what?
Well, it was a restaurant? No, it was more, more of a cafe. Mm-hmm. Strictly drinks.
Mm-hmm.
Uh, they had what you call a... Bansick. Oh, yeah. Yeah, you know Frisco.
Yeah.

Well, Frisco used to come in there and dance for dimes. I'm out money shilling for them. I shilled many times a quarter and didn't get it back. Yeah, I mean that. Sure. Uh, you see, we followed this, this gypsy ensemble that played soft, dreamy, gypsy music, you see. And when we come in there, the contrast is too great because those guys were blowing their brains out and everybody sitting there holding their ears. But, uh...
In other words, y'all didn't go over good right away.

No, we didn't go over good. They were sending, they were figuring about sending those rag, rag, rag, matazzy, jazzy guys back where they got them from. Smiley Corbin wouldn't even speak to us. He was so mad.
So then when did y'all catch on?

Well, uh, down the street, in the middle of the block, was the, uh, I'd say, I think it was Cones Grand Opera House. That was big time Waterville. And Bert Swann and Charlie Mack came to town. And so they came over there to hear this jazzy band. Incidentally, that's where that word jazz came from. Ah. Jazzy band. Clangy, jazzy, anything. Who put it on y'all? Do you remember? Well, who knows? It just grew up around Randolph and York. Were you in Chicago before y'all? No, no. They didn't even know how to spell it. They first spelled it J-A-Z, then J-A-Z-Z, then J-A-S, and J-A-S-S. And it finally stuck and was recognized, he'd tell me, by Webster, put it in the dictionary. It would. But that's where it originated from. Contrary to what Tommy Brown says about it, I know. I was there. That's where it originated. Uh-huh. I think that little fella, three years ago when I was in Chicago, with Sharky, I saw that same little Jewish guy, his old papers there. And he knows. He knows. He was in front of the lambs there? Yeah, on Clark Street, right on the corner. On Clark over there to look. Right on the corner. I went to look him up to see if he was still there. And he knows where the word jazz came from, too. Not 22nd Street.
What street was Lamb on?
On Randolph and Clark.
Right in the loop.

Oh, yeah. Right downtown. So, Bert Swore and Charlie Mack came in there. And a fella named John Wilmess was the manager. So they told Johnny Wilmess that, where did you get this band from? That's according to a Charlie Mack statement. He said, oh, don't say anything about them. We're sending them back. So Mack says, well, you're crazy. He said, this is something different. He said, you don't understand what these guys are doing. He said, they're really crazy. My type of music. So those are the bamboo blackface comedian? Oh yeah, the first one, Sworn Mac, Sworn Mac before Moran and Mac. Yeah. And they were big time performers too, headliners. So they got up there and they asked us if we knew the yellow dog rag, and that was their, one of their big numbers. So they got up on the floor and we played the yellow dog rag,
and they sang it, and that was it. Well, they began packing it in there? Oh yes. Do you have any other big time people from the show that came over there? Oh, it was loaded every night. It got to be,

it got to be an attraction, whereas one performer would ask the other if he heard that band over there. And they'd say, no, it's a go over here. Oh yeah, heavy Berlin and what's the name of these uh, dancers. Oh, it's right on the tip of my tongue right now. They were the big time dancers of all time around that. Man? No, uh, man and his wife. I remember her, Castle, Irene Castle. Uh huh. She used to come in there with a monkey on her shoulder, live monkey. And they danced a couple of times to the music and they said it was great. Well, we could have went with them, but who wanted to go? Nobody wanted to go. It wouldn't have been any better anyhow, because by that time, uh, everybody signed up except me to a contract. And I didn't want anybody to sign a contract because they said, these guys are smarter than you are. That fella named Joe Levy was booking agent. He gave a long syrupy talk, you know, and I was the only one who didn't sign a contract. I can prove that. The rest of them signed a contract. Sure, he offered us too much. I mean, uh, to leave that and go to New York, you mean? No, no, he, uh, uh, he, he, he would give us so much more money a week each three months. And we could do this and we could do that. And when it come time to sign the contract, read the contract, I guess I was the only one who read it. He was offering us nothing. So I said, well, I can do better without a contract. And that way I figured I could make him look up to me instead of me looking down to him. See? So, uh, because I, we weren't in a union at that time and I could quit on a moment's notice. And if I quit, then the band was hooked. No piano player, they couldn't play, that was for sure. Yeah, nobody up there was playing that style at all? Oh, no, no. Never heard of it.
No. Well, then how come you all left Lambs? Well, how long we had Lambs? Do you remember that?

Well, we started there on, uh, May 18th, 1915. And we were in New York in September. The reason for the New York fiasco and for ever leaving the Lambs was a fella named Harry Fitzgerald, a big booking agent from New York came there and he told us how swell the band was and everything. And he'd, uh, give us a world of the fence around it and didn't even see the fence. There's another guy I didn't sign a contract with. They did, but not me. I told him, no, I want to see this. I said, I want to see the money. Well, you got it. I said, no, I don't want any contract on anything else. I want to feel like anytime you don't come up with the amount of money you promised me, I'm going to either get that money or I'm not going to play. Because I was holding the reins that time. And the rest of them were too. They were in demand. So a bunch of jackasses, they give any notice. They sneaked out. They broke the contract. They ran away to New York and I knew that wasn't the right thing to do.
You mean the band? Yeah, the whole outfit. Well, who'd they take on base? And if you didn't go?
Well, no, I went with them, but I didn't want to go. I didn't want to break the contract ahead with, uh, Lambs? At the Lambs with Joe Levy. I told them. Have you been all right there? Oh, yes.
How did you live in Chicago while you were playing there?
Well, I lived several different places. I, where did I live? I lived at the Congress Hotel on Harrison and Wabash Avenue. That's an old time. It is probably out of business. Why not too?
Well, Congress is still going, but it's extended all the way over on Michigan now.
Uh, this hotel was on Wabash on the northwest corner.
All right. Well, now it's extending all the way to Michigan Avenue.

No, did I say Congress? That's not the, no, that's not the name of it. That's not the name of it. I can't. You were near, near your place of work. Well, about six blocks. I can't think right offhand, uh, what the name of that hotel was. Commercial. Commercial. That's the name of it. That's the name now.
Well, uh, Arnold, when, uh, when y'all went to New York, where'd you open up there?

Well, we, we went to New York. We were supposed to be in a town topic show. Or you had such celebrities as Trixie Ferganza and Lou Hearn, all big time star acts. And we were supposed to be on the stage with them. However, when we got there, we were supposed to be in a show. And I called these fellas' attention to the fact. I said, well, there's your Harry Fitzgerald. I said, you're supposed to be in the show. You're working in a restaurant. It was a monstrous place. The Century Theater. It was up at, uh, 62nd and Central Park West. And it took in a whole square. A whole square round. It wasn't the day I came in there. I didn't get lost. I'm telling you, I got lost every day. I'd have to ask somebody how I could find my way around. And, uh, after even the intermissions and stuff, I was afraid to leave there because the place was so big and there was so many dressing rooms and stage entrances and things that, well, I kept repeatedly
getting lost in the joint. But you're all hooking up in the restaurant instead of on the stage.

That's right. That's right. And then I called every attention to it. I said, well, where's this Harry Fitzgerald? You fellas signed your contracts with him. I said, I didn't sign anything with him. I got nothing to lose.
Well, did you have the same group with you then?
Same crowd. Sure.
Well, uh, Larry Shields wasn't with you then?

Oh, yes. Larry was with us. Well, then what became of Gus? Uh, what became of Gus? In the meantime, Bert Kelly was playing over at the Sherman Hotel, which was across the street from the Lambs. And Bert Kelly wanted a clarinet player like Gussie Miller. So, Raymond Lopez got in touch with Larry Shields and sent for him. Of course, Kelly paid the expense and all. And they brought Larry Shields up there. I hate to say this, but it's true. Larry Shields couldn't cut it with the band because the band was reading. You mean the, uh, Sherman House? Sherman House was reading all music. Larry couldn't play music. Whose band was that? Uh, Bert Kelly.
Uh, that's not Peg Kelly.
No, no, no. Bert Kelly, a banjo player.
Uh-huh.

And they, at that time, they had skating in the, in the Sherman Hotel, in the cocktail, well, cocktail line. It was, uh, restaurant and cafe. And, uh, so Bert Kelly came over and told Raymond about it, expressed his dissatisfaction. Gussie was listening. Gussie said, well, he said, I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take the job. And I guess the job paid twice as much money as we were getting. So, he said, was he a reader? Could he read? Gussie? Oh, yeah. Yeah. You remember I told you he was in a school orchestra when he was reading music?
Yeah, yeah.
So, Guss went in there and he swapped jobs, that's all. He just swapped Larry.
Was there all right feelings in the band?

No, no, no. It was agreed. Well, it, it, it, it was a thing to keep Larry Shields in Chicago. It keep from sending him back home. Mm-hmm. Because who could he play with? Mm-hmm. Except us. That was the only band he could play with. The rest of them all strictly Northmen.
Did he fit all right with you all?
Oh, sure. Sure.
Well, then, you stayed then at this, uh, restaurant in New York for how long?

Oh, I don't know. Approximately. Possibly four weeks. And that was it. In the meantime, I told Raymond, I said, we're, we're not going to make it here. These people not going for this stuff. So, we went down to Rising Webbers. It was up there. Sophie Tucker was on. It was a big place.
Uh-huh.

And, uh, Sophie Tucker was working upstairs. Mm-hmm. It was so big that it had a terrace around it. Mm-hmm. On the, uh, two-story. Mm-hmm. So, we saw Mr. Schultz. I'm pretty sure that was his name manager. Then we told him what we had. He said, all right. He said, I'll tell you what I'll do. He said, I'll give you boys a contract for two weeks and $25 a man a week. But after the money we're getting in Chicago, that was peanuts.
How much were you getting at, uh, what do you call it? The Century? Is that what you...
Um, oh, the Century Theater.
Century Theater. How much were you getting?

Well, we were getting $50, I think, a week. So, none of them were interested. We could have had all the gravy that the Dixieland Band got, because we were there before them, and we could have been hired before them. We could have worked the place. And, uh, I told them, well, we had a meeting. We talked it over, and I said, well, why don't we just go and take the job and wire Frisco? I said, we can pitch in, pitch in a couple of dollars a piece, and get Frisco up here to do that dance, that Frisco dance that he did. And his girlfriend, Loretta McDermott, had lived in New York, up in the Bronx, on the 53rd Street. And there'd been peaches for her right in the neighborhood. So, uh, the boys said, no, wasn't enough money. It wasn't this, it wasn't that. So, I said, all right, do what you please. And then we got out of the job. There wasn't anything else that was brewing around. Harry Fitzgerald turned out to be the kind of guy I thought he was. And so I got aboard a boat, United Fruit Company, liner, and came on down to New Orleans.
Well, when did you, didn't you travel with that group under the, uh, name, uh, in a vaudeville thing called
the, uh, Four or Five Rubes? Oh, the musical rubes, yeah. I'll take a look.
I forget where we were. Where's with the musical rubes? That's right. Yeah. That's right.

Well, how'd that come about? Well, uh, That was out of New York? That was in New York, yes. Uh-huh. So they, you see, the uniform originated in Chicago at the Lambs, so that musical rubes. Oh, yeah, to dress up and... Oh, sure, sure. They figured that they put a lot of corn shocks and a haystack and all of that. They, they figured that, uh, making rubes out of us was the proper thing in the big city. So, they started there. And they didn't call it musical rubes, they called it Brown Band from Dixieland. But then, when we played vaudeville up there, call it musical rubes. And the big city of New York didn't know what we were doing. They didn't? No, they were worse than Chicago. They were calling it, they, they, everything that wasn't good is what they called us. Clangy. How long were you, uh,
were you in the vaudeville thing for the musical rubes? Yeah. Yeah, we played, uh, oh, I guess it must

have been about a month at, uh, six weeks at the absolute most. They brought us from one end of New York. Was it a chain of, uh, a picture of shows? Yeah, the theater's own. They brought us from the north end to the south end and the crossover into Brooklyn and down in, uh, Long Island and everywhere. We were playing all the houses you never heard of. And the closest we ever got to the Ballad Theater was, we played one of those Sunday concerts. They used to have Sunday concerts in New York at that time, you know, and bought 10 acts for 50 cents. Place packed. Ah, well, one, one day we played the Columbia. Used to be a burlesque house on 47th and Broadway. That was right across the street, you might say, from the palace. Big shot. And we got a terrific hand. So we wondered what happened. How did we come to get this hand? So we started asking around. They come to find out that every music publisher and singer, you know, they used to have, uh, piano players or company singers to plug the song, pluggers, song pluggers at that time. Yeah. They were all in there. Ah. And they were the only ones that knew what we were doing. The audience didn't. So I guess when they started applauding, the audience took it up. Yeah. That was it. All you needed was a clack. Oh yeah. That night they all got together and they were talking about how much money they was going to charge. A couple of weeks later, I was on the boat. I told them, I don't want to fiddle around here with you guys. I says, if this is the way it's going to be, I says, I can do better in New Orleans, which I did. Of course. How long did you stay in New Orleans then? Well, you see, Gus Miller, when he found out that the band was breaking up, and it definitely was, yeah, he got a hold of Raymond Lopez. And Raymond went back to work with Kelly in Chicago. Bill Lambert came down here. Uh, Larry Shields came down here. And Tommy Brown, he went back to Chicago. He hooked on with Ray Miller, Black and White Melody Boys. So that really was the finish of Brown's band.
No head. But what year do you think that was? About 1915? No, that was 16. Yeah. Then,

I went back to Chicago with Happy Shillin. There's Happy Shillin and Georgie Borth, Johnny Fisher, and I and Johnny, let's say I think it was Johnny Frisco, who was the drummer. No, Williams was the drummer in that outfit. Then we went to work in a place called the Orsonia. Mike Fritzlant's joint on, it was all Madison near Paulina. And we did all right there until they booted us out of there. So we went down to the corner and went to work for Tommy Thomas. And everybody was well satisfied. You see, uh, Brown's band had already paved the way. And then the Dixieland band came in. Incidentally, that's where they got the name from the original Dixieland band, because everybody said, there's another Dixieland band in town. They worked on 35th Street, Shillin. And, uh, it wasn't hard to break through in, uh, 1916. I'm pretty sure it was 16. Well, I went back there with the other band, with Shillin. So we lived on Warren Avenue in Paulina. One morning I got up, wasn't it, it was about 10 o'clock, because they closed up at one o'clock. They had a one o'clock closing law in Chicago. And a woman sitting on the front porch that I had talked with told me, says, uh, what happened? Did you boys finish up over at the corner? I said, not that I know of. She said, well, three of your boys are gone. And they were. And they were. Happy Shillin. Happy Shillin. And left? Just picked up and left. Told, didn't even tell me.
Who was managing that, uh? Happy Shillin. He and Fisher left? And, uh, Freddie Williams. Uh-huh.

Piano player Williams? Yeah. And, uh. Wanted to come back to New Orleans? Uh, no, Williams was a drummer. Yeah, they came back. Williams, uh. You were playing the piano with them still? Yeah. Uh-huh. Georgie Barth was a trumpet player. So I, I looked around and I asked the woman landlady, let's take a look at their room. And sure enough, so I went over to the cafe and the colored fella cleaning up. And I asked him, he said, oh, he come in, took the drums and everything. I didn't know a thing about it. So I was hooked. I went to see Tommy Thomas. So Tommy said, well, what are we going to do? I said, I don't know. I said, I just can't go out in the park and pick up men. But I said, if we can get along for tonight and tomorrow night, I feel confident. What did you have? Uh, did you have anybody? Uh, yeah,
just two of them left? Oh, no, just me. Yeah, there are three or four of them at Goldman? Sure. All the band left

but me. Left me high and dry. So I told him in a couple of nights, I can get you another Dixieland band. I feel confident that I can. So I got in touch with my brother Jack and told him to get a hold of some of the fellas that he thought could play. So he got a hold of four other guys and I wired them the money and they caught the train and came on. A fella named Weber played clarinet. Freddie New Roth played trumpet. Red Rolling played clarinet later. Jack played trombone. And Johnny Frisco played drums and I played piano. So he was only without his Dixieland music for two nights and luckily they started on a Friday. The two big nights were yet to come, see. So he really didn't lose anything. Well, you all worked there how long? Oh, for Tommy, we worked there a long while. I guess about, uh, year and a half worked for Tommy. You weren't married then, huh? No. Then along came the war. I'll hold it right there.

You mentioned a couple that I had completely forgotten about. This is September the 29th, 1956. We're at 815 Eileen Street, New Orleans, Louisiana. An informal interview with Mr. Arnold Iacana. This is real two. Continue. Now, Arnold, we were just about beginning to talk about when you had, uh, brought these bunch of boys up from New Orleans to play, uh, when there's a bunch of skip town on you. Yeah. Yeah. Well, uh, you say you played there about a year and a half? Uh, that was Tommy Thomas's,

yes. What did you all call yourself? Well, the Crescent City Jazz Band. Uh-huh. From New Orleans, of Crescent City. You were the leader? Oh, leader. What such a leader as he was. Everybody was a leader. Played a double, huh? No, no. I was just a guy that coaxed all the trouble onto myself and, uh, got in between the boss and the band. I was in the middle all the time. They, uh, for a while everything was great. Then he wanted a raise. I went to the boss and tried to get a raise and I couldn't. Oh, then we should look for another job. Or we should look for another job. And I was the guy that had to get up, watch out there. I was the guy that had to get up in the morning and look for another job for them. Cold freezing mornings and everything else and getting nothing out of it. So I figured, well, shucks, I'm not, I'm not going to get up and look for jobs either. So the band drifted apart. They worked at, uh, uh, Mickey Frank's tile bar. That was a place on, uh, on Clark street and Ohio. Clark and Ohio. Well, we had a good job there. Everything was going great. All right. Yeah, everything was going great until the guy started. They, they, we used to operate on Sunday, Sunday night. Of course, it was against the law, but you know, they used to operate anyhow. And they had a service bar, a special service bar. And up above that special service bar, they had, uh, some cupboards up there loaded with whiskey. And they had a hair spa on the thing. And if you stuck your hand in there, which you could, you could pull out a pint of whiskey. Well, I didn't know those fellows were stealing the man's whiskey. Your boys and your
family? Yeah. I was wondering how much drinking they were doing. Well, they weren't doing much

drinking on the job because I didn't allow it. They, they, they got paid to work. Now I want them to work. And so they, I didn't mind if they took drinks, but nobody got drunk. I didn't want that. So the man come to me and gave him a two weeks notice. I said, what for? He said, you got thieves in your band. He said, you've been stealing all my whiskey. So are you.

I didn't want that. So, the band come to me and gave him a two weeks notice. I said, what for? He said, you got thieves in your band. He said, you been stealing all my whiskey. So he opened up the thing and showed me all the whiskey gone. I didn't know who took it. So the only thing I could do would be to, uh, the only thing I could do would be to, uh,

And the fella's description tallied with Rap. Although I know Rap didn't do it because Rap was working with us. He couldn't have done it. So one night Rap don't show up. He comes up missing and everybody's wondering. He got a hold of his wife and said, I don't know where he is. He went to work and all this. So I got a hold of the police department and told them that Rap would answer to the description of this guy almost. And I said, I think he's lost his memory. They had a lapse of memory. And I said, if you see him, don't shoot him. Just pick him up. And I said, my name and address and telephone. If you call me, I'll come down and identify him first. So they finally caught him. He was in a grocery store, combination grocery and fruit. He was eating bananas, picking them off the stalk. So the banana people, the man that owned the place, he didn't know who Rap was. But he had read the description of the burglar, highwayman. And one day The only trouble though, you see, he hopped one of his clarinets for a pistol. And he had that pistol in his pocket. And we had an awful lot of talking to do to get him squared up. Of course, it was easy when we got the manager of the ballroom to go down in McCluskey.
He testified he was playing. He went down, sure.
He went down to the police station and, well, he's a well-known man around town anyhow. And I think that possibly he's...
That was in Minneapolis? Yes. What year? Do you remember?
Well, no. I can't just say offhand what year it was.
It wasn't 1920, was it?

No. Later than that? Yeah, that was about 30... Oh, I'd say 38. Maybe 39. About that time. It'd be about that time. Uh... No, on second thought, I'm pretty positive it was in the fall of 1924. Or possibly 25, but I'm pretty positive it was in 1924 that we were in Minneapolis.
Do you remember the name of the place where you played up there?
We played the Marigold Ballroom. Uh-huh.
Yeah.
Uh, I also slipped up on a good one. What's that?
Sig Meyers Band.

Oh, you tell me about it. You asked me some time ago about what happened when I left the Playhouse. Well, I worked the Playhouse. Well, I worked the Playhouse. And it was through the New Orleans Rhythm King at Friars Inn that I went to work with Sig Meyers. Uh, when Sig approached me about the thing, he didn't offer me much money, but he offered me a short job. And that was, uh, 8.30 till 12. It was five sessions a week. Uh, Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday night, Sunday night, and Sunday afternoon. Three hours on Sunday afternoon. So I kept dickering back and forth with Sig Meyers about the job. I told him I didn't need the job. He needed me worse than I needed the job. So we finally got, we finally got together and we finally, I finally settled for $95 a week. And I was there a couple of months with him and he gave me $5 raise because I knew that other fellas were getting $100. And I knew Don Gooden well that what I added to the band was worth the other five and Sig knew it. So I just added it.
Was that a big band, huh?
Oh, yes. It was ten men.
That was the day when the swing was starting to come in.

Oh, yeah. Uh-huh. Ten men. They had, oh, Sig had some good men in his band. He had fellas like Bollie DeFoe, Muxi Spania, uh, uh, Bob Buscelli. I haven't heard much of him recently. He, wait, in the last 20 years or so, I think Bob had just wrapped up. He went in for the motion picture business. He didn't care too much about the, uh, music. Shorty Williamson, Georgie Petroni, Earl Andrews. Sig played fiddle. Sig played fiddle, yes. I was with the band, too. Did he double on anything else? No. A good part of the time he just waved his bow. Uh-huh. But Sig was a good school musician. Uh-huh. I think that he could have... Well, you were with him a long time, aren't you? I was with him, uh, 53 months. Good night. Uh, have you ever heard a fellow named Marvin Saxby? Yeah. Well, Saxby was the guitar player. Uh, Saxby was an exceptional, outstanding guy at that time. As a matter of fact, uh, when, uh, the first amplifiers came out, uh, Lyon and Healey hired Sykesby to demonstrate him in the afternoon. And I understand the pay was pretty good. Of course, I don't know what he got, but he said he was getting well paid. So I stayed with Sig four years and five months. And then my good friend Muggsy, he was causing me to leave in Sig. Because, uh, you see, I was the highest priced man in the band. After all those years. I was getting real money. And Sig paid in check. I made the mistake one night of cashing my check at the drugstore on the corner. And, uh, devil-faced Muggsy Spania saw it. And that started the trouble. Uh, Sig didn't want me to quit, but I told him I didn't want to work with people like that. And I knew he wouldn't fire Muggsy. So, all right. Rap work with Sig, too, you know. Rap over. Oh, yeah. And the same band with you? No, I didn't. You know, no, it was just before I joined him. Uh, Sig had about the fastest band in Chicago at that time.
Was Rapolo a reader, too?
No. No, huh? No, he couldn't read it. No big as a bass player.
How did he play a sax? Did you like his sax style?
Well, he played all right, but I heard better. You liked his clarinet playing?
Better.
Much better, yeah.
Have you ever heard him and Charlie Cardello wait together? No.
Never have. No, I don't think I have. I don't remember it.

Because those were the last records that Rap was on with the Halfway House, you see. Uh-huh. And that's when Charlie was telling me some cute things that happened with Rap. Uh-huh. That he got mad and didn't show up for a session. They had a recording session, you know? Yeah.
Yeah.

And Rap's brother came down there with a gun on his hip and he told Cardello, who was going to play clarinet instead of Rapolo. Uh-huh. Says, if you copy any of his style, I'll be standing out here waiting for you.
Well, you see, that gives you some slight idea of how, uh, of how serious they were about musicians and the music played.

Well, one thing that keeps coming to my mind, and I'm glad I thought of it before this tape runs out, I noticed, looking at all the old records, which is the only way that I can really look back and remember these fellas, the number of times the same fellas played with different bands. Was it because they were having fights and squabbles and quitting and going to somebody else or what?

Well, uh, if the records were made here, uh, some of these bands still adhered to the old principle. They hired the same man to play with three, four, five different bands because he's good. Uh-huh. Because they think he's the best. Uh-huh. But there is no such a thing as the best.

Well, you know what I'm trying to lead up to is this. You take what's going on in your audience today, it's the same damn thing. You'll find the same musician's name with all different kinds of bands.
Yeah. Because they think he's the best.
No, sometimes you hear him around you, I wouldn't play with so many people.

Oh. You know that kind of business? Yeah, that's just so much talk. I've heard it too. Wow. They call, uh, they call the man all kind of dirty names and everything else. They wouldn't play with him, uh, like Chink Martin. He said he wouldn't play with Sharky again if he was the last man in the world.
Well, what happened between them? Well, I don't know.

But when I saw Chink Martin on Royal Street and he was working with Sharky, I said, what happened? The world's coming to an end, Sharky, but you told me that you wouldn't, uh, work with Sharky if he was the last man in the world. I said, you must be all by yourself. He walked away. He didn't ask me or anything. He just walked away. And I, I think he's sore at me ever since. He's not with Sharky on this trip, is he?
No, no.
You know who Sharky's got with him? I don't know.
Uh, Buddy Frank.
Oh, has he? Yeah.
And Buddy Frank.
Well, I don't know who else. Somebody told me. I, I don't know. I didn't even see him. Somebody.
I just found out last week that he was gone because I've got his sister-in-law, Mrs. Ziegler, and Mercy, who, between life and death, a heart attack.
Uh, I didn't know he was gone either.
Tell me he won't be back until after the next year because he's, he's got contracts. He's not. He's not.
Central America trip?
No, he's going to Canada. Oh.
Yeah. Well, he's all right. He's all right as far as the word goes. But he's another crazy guy. I don't understand that.
That boy's a fine trumpet player. I don't understand.

Doc, he don't know when he's well off. That's his trouble. That's right. He won't, uh, he thinks what he don't know, nobody else knows. But as far as travel and experience on the road, not only with bands, with shows, with, with almost every kind of entertainment, I could, uh, give them cards and spades and beat them because I, I, all in total, I spent about 12, 15 years just on the road alone. So I know it done good and well, yes.
What other, uh, businesses have you been in other than the musician business?

Well, that's all except for a year and a half I worked for the government. But, uh, I never cared for anything else but music. I preferred to play music because it was easy, because the remuneration was big, and, uh, it was a clean job. And except for a few cafes where I had to inhale all that smoke and stink every night, my jobs were mostly in dance halls or in, uh, theaters. Because I picked them that way. I didn't try to jump the gun. I waited until the job was open and then I applied for it or they asked me. I, I wanted to stay out of cafes, you see. I worked for a long time in Henry Gendron, but he worked the cream of the crop because he was working for Boucher. And, uh, Boucher has one of the most beautiful, I think it's the most beautiful cafe in the world, out there in Northbrook, Illinois. The grounds, uh, well, the grounds are worth better than a million dollars alone. It's a beautiful place. And I've never seen it. Oh, I haven't seen any, any cafe until you see that. That's really big. He has a, he has a river running through his property. A small river. And he has his, uh, gondolas and gondoliers dressed like Italians. They are Italians, but dressed just like over in Naples in Italy. And they ride the people up and down on the river at night in those gondolas. You ever been to Europe? Oh, yeah.
With a band or? No, not with no band.
No, I was over there with the army.
Uh, Arnold, did, have you ever been, uh, stranded any place? No. You mean, uh, with no money? With not being going to get home? Oh, no.

Oh, no. How many musicians had to ride all the while? Like I told you before. And sent a collect telegrams. With Brown's band. I always, even until, until today, if I go to Jackson, Mississippi, or, or 200 miles or 400 miles, I always want to have enough in my pocket that I won't have to walk. So that I ride back. That I won't have to take and, uh, thumb my way on highways either. Or else if I can't make it that way, I won't go. Uh-huh. If I go to Jackson, Mississippi, or 200 miles or 400 miles, I always want to have enough in my pocket that I won't have to walk, that I ride back. I won't have to take and thumb my way on highways either, or else if I can't make it that way, I won't go. I never was where I had to go.

I've been sweating you for almost two hours, and I think we're going to call it today, and thank you so very much, because I realize I've just begun to scratch the surface of all your store of knowledge. We had hoped to have Bud, Loyer County, in on this, but he lives across the river, and I couldn't get over there. I have an obstetrical case that may bust loose. So we're going to resume this another time when we can have the two of them together, Arnold, Loyer County, and Bud, where they will probably stimulate each other into much more memories than we have. Now, surely, thank you.
Yeah. You bring up some names that I don't know, I guess. Thanks again, Arnold. You're entirely welcome, Doc.
